query: For initially solid FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles exposed to the premelting and melting regime, the limited understanding of their thermal response prevents clear definition of their usable temperature range and behavior during high-temperature synthesis. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs the onset and progression of their phase transition and why? Specify a controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to the starting baseline, relevant boundary conditions, supporting evidence from prior nanoparticle studies, and a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles, the onset and inward progression of melting is triggered by thermally activated surface segregation—predominantly of Cu—which locally reduces the melting point at the nanoparticle surface. When the surface diffusion of Cu is uninhibited, early premelting appears at the surface and propagates into the core.
generation.material_initial_state: Solid, homogeneous FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles with a randomized elemental distribution.
generation.intervention: Heat the nanoparticles incrementally in an inert atmosphere and compare nanoparticles with bare surfaces to nanoparticles with a surface passivation layer that restricts surface atomic diffusion.
generation.conditions: Experiments performed in the premelting to melting temperature regime (above ~0.8 times the bulk melting temperature) in an inert gas environment on nanoparticles in the tens-of-nanometers size range.
generation.structural_mediator: A surface compositional gradient marked by enrichment of Cu at the nanoparticle surface.
generation.mechanism: Upon heating, the lower-melting-point Cu atoms diffuse toward the surface, creating regions with a depressed local melting point. This initiates surface premelting, which then propagates inward as temperature increases.
generation.predicted_outcome: Nanoparticles with unpassivated surfaces will display an earlier onset of surface melting accompanied by detectable Cu enrichment (via in-situ TEM/EDX), whereas passivated nanoparticles will show a more uniform melting onset near the bulk melting temperature.
generation.baseline: Nanoparticles that remain compositionally homogeneous (e.g., through effective surface passivation) exhibit a uniform melting onset corresponding to the bulk composition.
generation.boundary: This mechanism applies specifically to high-entropy alloy nanoparticles with typical sizes in the tens-of-nanometers range under inert or high-vacuum conditions; deviations may occur for significantly larger particles or under reactive environments.
generation.uncertainty: The precise temperature differential and kinetics of the surface premelting process remain to be quantified under various nanoparticle sizes and passivation schemes.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles: one with naturally exposed surfaces and one with a surface passivation coating to inhibit Cu and other atoms from diffusing. Incrementally heat the samples under an inert atmosphere while monitoring the onset of melting and local elemental compositions using in-situ TEM and EDX.
measurements: Temperature at which surface premelting is first observed
Spatial elemental mapping to detect Cu enrichment
Global melting onset and progression kinetics
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If passivated nanoparticles do not show a delayed onset of surface melting relative to unpassivated ones or if no significant Cu enrichment is observed at the surfaces of unpassivated nanoparticles prior to bulk melting, the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractHigh entropy alloys (HEAs) are an important new material class with significant application potential in catalysis and electrocatalysis. The entropy-driven formation of HEA materials requires high temperatures and controlled cooling rates. However, catalysts in general also require highly dispersed materials, i.e., nanoparticles. Only then a favorable utilization of the expensive raw materials can be achieved. Several recently reported HEA nanoparticle synthesis strategies, therefore, avoid the high-temperature regime to prevent particle growth. In our work, we investigate a system of five noble metal single-source precursors with superior catalytic activity for the oxygen reduction reaction. Combining in situ X-ray powder diffraction with multi-edge X-ray absorption spectroscopy, we address the fundamental question of how single-phase HEA nanoparticles can form at low temperatures. It is demonstrated that the formation of HEA nanoparticles is governed by stochastic principles and the inhibition of precursor mobility during the formation process favors the formation of a single phase. AbstractRefractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are emerging materials with potential for use under extreme conditions. As a newly developed material system, a comprehensive understanding of their long-term stability under potential service temperatures remains to be established. This study examined a titanium-vanadium-niobium-tantalum alloy, a promising RHEA known for its superior high-temperature strength and room-temperature ductility. Using a combination of advanced analytical microscopies, Calculation of Phase Diagrams (CALPHAD) software, and nanoindentation, we investigated the evolution of its microstructure and mechanical properties upon aging at 700°C. Trace interstitials such as oxygen and nitrogen, initially contributing to solid solution strengthening, promote phase segregation during thermal aging. As a result of the depletion of solute interstitials within the metal matrix, a progressive softening is observed in the alloy as a function of aging time. This study, therefore, underscores the need for a better control of impurities in future development and application of RHEAs. AbstractRapid synthesis of high-entropy alloy nanoparticles (HEA NPs) offers new opportunities to develop functional materials in widespread applications. Although some methods have successfully produced HEA NPs, these methods generally require rigorous conditions such as high pressure, high temperature, restricted atmosphere, and limited substrates, which impede practical viability. In this work, we report laser solid-phase synthesis of CrMnFeCoNi nanoparticles by laser irradiation of mixed metal precursors on a laser-induced graphene (LIG) support with a 3D porous structure. The CrMnFeCoNi nanoparticles are embraced by several graphene layers, forming graphene shell-encapsulated HEA nanoparticles. The mechanisms of the laser solid-phase synthesis of HEA NPs on LIG supports are investigated through theoretical simulation and experimental observations, in consideration of mixed metal precursor adsorption, thermal decomposition, reduction through electrons from laser-induced thermionic emission, and liquid beads splitting. AbstractDirect formation of ultra-small nanoparticles on carbon supports by rapid high temperature synthesis method offers new opportunities for scalable nanomanufacturing and the synthesis of stable multi-elemental nanoparticles. However, the underlying mechanisms affecting the dispersion and stability of nanoparticles on the supports during high temperature processing remain enigmatic. In this work, we report the observation of metallic nanoparticles formation and stabilization on carbon supports through in situ Joule heating method. We find that the formation of metallic nanoparticles is associated with the simultaneous phase transition of amorphous carbon to a highly defective turbostratic graphite (T-graphite). Molecular dynamic (MD) simulations suggest that the defective T-graphite provide numerous nucleation sites for the nanoparticles to form. Furthermore, the nanoparticles partially intercalate and take root on edge planes, leading to high binding energy on support. This interaction between nanoparticles and T-graphite substrate strengthens the anchoring and provides excellent thermal stability to the nanoparticles. drafts.hypothesis: The onset of phase transition in FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy nanoparticles is driven by thermally activated surface segregation, in which lower-melting-point constituents (such as Cu) preferentially migrate to the surface. This local compositional change reduces the melting point at the nanoparticle surfaces, initiating premelting that progressively invades the more compositionally uniform core with further temperature increase.
drafts.material_initial_state: Solid FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy nanoparticles with a randomized elemental distribution.
drafts.intervention: Heat the nanoparticles incrementally in an inert atmosphere while comparing particles with naturally exposed surfaces versus those with a surface passivation treatment designed to inhibit elemental migration.
drafts.conditions: Experiments conducted in the premelting to melting temperature regime (e.g., above ~0.8 Tm for the bulk alloy) under inert gas conditions to avoid oxidation or chemical contamination; nanoparticle size should be maintained in the tens-of-nanometers range.
drafts.structural_mediator: Elemental surface segregation that creates a compositional gradient with an enrichment of lower melting point elements at the nanoparticle surface.
drafts.mechanism: Elevated temperatures stimulate diffusion of certain elements (especially the lower-melting-point ones) toward the surface. This segregation lowers the local melting point at the surface relative to the core, initiating localized premelting. As temperature further rises, the melting front propagates inward as thermally induced homogenization occurs.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Nanoparticles without surface passivation are expected to show an earlier onset of surface premelting (as detected by in-situ TEM or localized calorimetry), with a distinct compositional gradient at the surface relative to the well-passivated counterparts that delay such segregation. Compared to the baseline of uniformly melting nanoparticles, the unpassivated particles will initiate melting at a lower temperature at their surfaces and show a more gradual progression toward complete melting.
drafts.baseline: Nanoparticles that maintain a homogeneous elemental distribution (either through inherent stability or via surface passivation) should exhibit a more uniform melting onset corresponding to the bulk melting point.
drafts.boundary: The hypothesis applies primarily to nanoparticles in the tens-of-nanometers size range under inert atmosphere conditions; deviations may occur with significant size changes or under reactive (oxidative) conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles: one set with naturally exposed surfaces and another set with a surface passivation coating designed to restrict elemental diffusion. Incrementally heat both sets in an inert gas atmosphere while performing in-situ TEM imaging coupled with energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDX) to monitor both structural changes and surface composition evolution.
measurements: Temperature at which surface premelting first occurs (via in-situ TEM)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If surface passivation does not result in a delayed onset of surface melting compared to unpassivated nanoparticles, or if no significant compositional gradient (indicative of elemental segregation) is observed before melting in the unpassivated samples, the hypothesis is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: The onset and progression of melting in solid FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles is governed by thermally activated surface segregation—specifically, a preferential enrichment of Cu at the nanoparticle surface lowers the local melting temperature and initiates a surface‐to‐core melting progression.
drafts.material_initial_state: Homogeneously mixed, solid FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles with uniformly distributed elemental composition.
drafts.intervention: Subject nanoparticles to a controlled heating regime entering the premelting and melting temperature range; compare nanoparticles with natural surfaces versus those with an inert passivation layer that hinders surface atom migration.
drafts.conditions: Identical inert atmosphere conditions with a standardized thermal ramp rate applied to both unpassivated and passivated nanoparticles, and nanoparticle sizes in a similar range (e.g., 5–50 nm).
drafts.structural_mediator: Local compositional inhomogeneity induced by Cu segregation to the nanoparticle surface.
drafts.mechanism: As the nanoparticles are heated, thermal energy promotes the migration of Cu atoms—which have a lower melting point compared to the other elements—from the interior to the surface. This segregation creates a Cu-enriched surface layer with a depressed melting point compared to the core. The resulting liquid layer then propagates inward, driving the progression of the phase transition.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Unpassivated nanoparticles are expected to exhibit earlier onset of surface premelting at lower temperatures, evidenced by the appearance of a liquid-like layer, compared to passivated nanoparticles where surface segregation is suppressed. Energy-dispersive analysis should reveal an increased Cu concentration at surfaces of unpassivated particles during premelting.
drafts.baseline: Nanoparticles with a homogeneous elemental distribution (as synthesized) that are heated under identical conditions without any surface modification, providing a standard melting onset temperature without pronounced surface effects.
drafts.boundary: This mechanism is expected to be significant for nanoparticles within the 5–50 nm range and in inert (non-oxidative) environments. Variations in particle size or changes to ambient conditions might alter the segregation dynamics and melting behavior.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two batches of FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles: one with the native surface and a second batch coated with a thin, inert passivation layer (e.g., SiO2) to block surface atom migration. Heat both batches under identical conditions in an inert atmosphere while monitoring temperature, structural changes, and elemental distributions.
measurements: In situ transmission electron microscopy (TEM) to observe the onset and progression of the liquid phase at the nanoparticle surfaces.
Energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDX) to track elemental (especially Cu) distribution as a function of temperature.
Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) to determine the melting onset temperature for both nanoparticle batches.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the unpassivated nanoparticles do not exhibit an earlier or more pronounced surface melting (evidenced by similar onset temperatures and lack of Cu enrichment at the surface) relative to the passivated nanoparticles, then the hypothesis that surface segregation (particularly of Cu) governs the phase transition will be falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: The phase transition in FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles is initiated by selective premelting at Cu‐rich regions on the nanoparticle surfaces. Because Cu has a lower melting point than the other constituent metals, even in an otherwise homogeneous high-entropy alloy, slight local enrichments or surface defects may promote early liquid formation. These Cu‐rich liquid pools then act as nucleation sites that trigger the propagation of melting throughout the nanoparticle.
drafts.material_initial_state: Solid, single‐phase FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy nanoparticles with an apparently homogeneous elemental distribution at room temperature.
drafts.intervention: Apply a controlled, gradual temperature ramp (e.g., using in situ TEM or a differential scanning calorimeter with rapid elemental mapping capabilities) to push the material into the premelting and melting regime. In parallel, compare with nanoparticles that have slightly reduced Cu content.
drafts.conditions: Experiments conducted in an inert or high vacuum environment to minimize oxidation, with heating rates slow enough to capture onset of local melting. Nanoparticles should be similarly sized and processed for fair comparison, and one control group should have modified (lower) Cu content.
drafts.structural_mediator: Localized Cu-enriched domains (or defect sites) on the nanoparticle surfaces that reduce the local melting point.
drafts.mechanism: Due to the lower bulk melting point of Cu compared to Fe, Ni, Cr, and Co, any slight elemental segregation or surface defects concentrate Cu and facilitate localized premelting. The formation of these liquid pools reduces the energy barrier for neighboring atoms to diffuse, leading to a rapid propagation of melting once nucleation has occurred.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Under controlled heating, initial melting will be observed at the nanoparticle surfaces as liquid domains that are enriched in Cu, visible through compositional mapping. Nanoparticles with a higher relative Cu content should exhibit an onset of premelting at lower temperatures relative to those with reduced Cu.
drafts.baseline: Nanoparticles maintained in a purely solid, single-phase crystalline state observed at temperatures well below any premelting effects, with uniform elemental distribution.
drafts.boundary: This mechanism applies to FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles synthesized under comparable conditions, in inert atmospheres and with similar particle sizes. The hypothesis is bounded by the assumption that even nominally homogeneous high-entropy alloys can exhibit subtle local compositional variations or defect sites that facilitate selective melting.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct an in situ heating experiment on FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles using TEM coupled with energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDX) mapping. Track the evolution of elemental distribution and local phase changes during controlled heating. In addition, perform the same test on nanoparticles with a reduced Cu content as a control.
measurements: Temperature at which localized liquid domains form on the nanoparticle surface
Spatial elemental mapping (especially Cu enrichment) during the onset of melting
Time-resolved imaging of the propagation of melting from the surface inward
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If no early formation of Cu-enriched liquid domains is detected prior to complete melting, or if changing the Cu content does not affect the melting onset temperature or melting propagation behavior, then the hypothesis is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: In FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles, the onset and progression of the phase transition during premelting are governed by surface-driven atomic reordering that locally reduces configurational entropy through elemental segregation, thereby nucleating localized melting which then propagates into the nanoparticle core.
drafts.material_initial_state: Solid, homogeneous, single-phase FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles with uniformly dispersed elements
drafts.intervention: Expose identical nanoparticle samples to a controlled high-temperature ramp in an inert or high-vacuum environment, comparing as-synthesized nanoparticles to those with an engineered surface passivation (e.g., a thin carbon coating) designed to restrict surface atomic mobility.
drafts.conditions: Controlled heating from ambient up through the premelting and melting regimes under high-vacuum or inert gas to prevent oxidation; nanoparticle sizes maintained in the nano-scale range (e.g., <20 nm) to ensure high surface-to-volume ratios.
drafts.structural_mediator: Surface atomic ordering and local elemental segregation which reduce configurational entropy at the nanoparticle surface
drafts.mechanism: At elevated temperatures, atoms at the nanoparticle surface become mobile and begin to segregate based on their individual melting points. This reordering lowers the local entropy stabilization at the surface, leading to the nucleation of localized liquid regions (premelting). These liquid zones then coalesce and progressively invade the core, resulting in complete melting.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Nanoparticles with unmodified surfaces will exhibit earlier and more pronounced localized melting at lower temperatures, with observable liquid domains forming at the surface. In contrast, surface-passivated nanoparticles that limit atomic diffusion will show delayed melting onset and a more uniform, higher temperature melting transition relative to the baseline.
drafts.baseline: Nanoparticles that remain fully solid with homogeneous elemental distribution and stable high configurational entropy, showing no evidence of localized premelting at lower high-temperature exposures.
drafts.boundary: This mechanism is expected to dominate in nanoparticles with high surface-to-volume ratios under inert or vacuum conditions; the role of surface segregation might differ in larger particles or in oxidizing environments where additional effects could arise.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles: one set with pristine surfaces and another with surface passivation (e.g., a carbon coating) intended to inhibit atomic diffusion. Heat both sets under identical high-vacuum conditions using a controlled temperature ramp, and monitor their structural evolution in situ via transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and high-temperature X-ray diffraction (XRD).
measurements: In situ TEM imaging to detect the onset and spatial distribution of liquid (premelted) regions
XRD analysis to track phase changes and melting onset temperature
X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) to assess surface elemental segregation patterns
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If both the passivated and unmodified nanoparticles exhibit similar melting onset temperatures, similar progression of premelting and no significant differences in surface elemental profiles, then the hypothesis that surface-mediated local entropy reduction and segregation triggers the premelting would be falsified.
